_comment: Starter RU<->EN idiom lexicon for the Detection Agent's idiom_lookup tool (agents/tools.py). Seeded 2026-09-20 from idioms that actually appeared in stage_a/stage_b batch 1-3 data plus the calibration notes from Stage B verification -- NOT exhaustive. Expand by appending entries as new idioms turn up in future batches; each entry's 'literal_survives' field records the batch-3 finding that some idioms carry their full charge through a literal/direct translation (so has_subtext should be false) while others genuinely need the idiomatic gloss (has_subtext true). See config/calibration_guidelines.md for the full reasoning behind literal_survives.

entries.literal_en: what the devil / what the hell (literal)
entries.note: Batch 3 calibration: exasperated-anger charge carries through direct translation -- has_subtext=false even with informal address alongside it.
Same pattern as какого чёрта -- direct idiomatic translation preserves the charge.
Resigned-fatalism idiom, survives direct translation per batch 3 calibration.

entries.idiomatic_en: to live with it / come to terms with it
entries.note: Resigned-fatalism idiom, survives direct translation per batch 3 calibration.

entries.idiomatic_en: looks like it's going to rain
entries.note: Plain weather idiom. Batch 1: a model's claim this alluded to Winnie-the-Pooh was rejected as unverified/fabricated -- kept here as a reminder to distrust unverified cultural-reference claims from generators.
Litotes -- survives direct/literal translation intact (batch 2 calibration: 'not the worst option' pattern).

entries.idiomatic_en: please, call me [informal] / drop the formalities
entries.note: Batch 3: a sentence *about* the ty/vy distinction itself is one of the clearest genuine has_subtext=true idiom/formality cases -- the Russian pronoun choice has no English lexical equivalent and must be glossed, not just translated.
